title: The Quiet Leadership Crisis AI Is About to Expose
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss newsletter argues that AI is in the process of dissolving the cover that has allowed weak leaders to pass as effective ones for decades: the camouflage of busyness. For years, the appearance of leadership -- running meetings, drafting reports, responding to emails at impressive speeds -- was nearly indistinguishable from actual leadership impact, because organizations had no clean way to decouple activity from effectiveness. AI is systematically automating that administrative output, which means the remaining visible work in a leadership role is the non-automatable core: coaching, hard conversations, trust-building, and steady presence in difficult moments. The article argues this is not a crisis caused by AI but a crisis AI is revealing -- the exposure of a distinction (management activity vs. leadership impact) that should have been made long ago. Leaders who were doing the real work all along will finally be seen; those who were occupying leadership-shaped roles will be publicly exposed. The author's practical advice: audit your week for the ratio of task execution to genuine leadership, find the hard conversation you have been avoiding, and stop hiding behind busyness before AI surfaces the gap for you.
points: * AI is not taking leadership roles; it is eliminating the administrative cover -- the busyness of meetings, decks, and email -- that allowed people occupying leadership positions to look effective without actually leading. * The distinction AI exposes is between management output (which AI can now replicate faster and more thoroughly) and leadership impact (trust-building, coaching, hard conversations) -- work that produces categorically different outcomes. * Leaders who were doing the real work all along -- trust-building, coaching, hard conversations, steady presence in difficult moments -- will finally be seen for what they were actually contributing, possibly for the first time. * The practical diagnostic: audit your week and ask what fraction of it was task execution versus genuine leadership activity -- if AI could do most of your week, your week was not mostly leadership. * The author's warning: get honest about your leadership impact while there is still time to close the gap, before AI closes it for you -- and when it does, it will be very publicly, in front of your whole team.
quotes: For decades, the busywork of management has provided a kind of camouflage. If you were constantly in meetings, constantly writing decks, constantly responding to emails and Slack, you looked like a leader. Your volume of activity covered the depth of impact.

Nobody had the tools, or frankly, the desire, to decouple doing a lot of management tasks from actually leading people well. The two got bundled together, and most organizations never bothered to unbundle them.

The crisis I'm talking about isn't that AI is going to take away leadership roles. The real crisis is that a large number of people currently occupying leadership roles have been getting credit for management output, not leadership impact, and that distinction is getting exposed to everyone.

Some leaders will discover, in a fairly public way, that they don't have much left once their task list is automated and managed by AI tools. Some teams are going to realize that the person who looked like their leader for years was mostly just... busy.

Some leaders, the ones who were doing the real work all along, the trust-building, the coaching, the hard conversations, the steady presence in difficult moments, are finally going to get seen for what they were actually contributing. Maybe even for the first time.

You need to get honest about your leadership impact while there's still time to close the gap, before AI closes it for you. And when it does, which will be sooner than you think, it will be very publicly, in front of your whole team.

For years, busyness was a reasonable proxy for leadership impact, because we had no better way to measure it. With AI, that proxy is disappearing, and what's left is the only thing that ever actually mattered: whether you made the people around you better.
